sentences.text: Lythronax was a massive predator estimated to reach lengths between 5 and 8 meters and weigh between 0.5 and 2.5 tonnes.
Its most prominent feature was a set of front teeth that grew to nearly 13 centimeters in length.
Unlike most of its relatives, this animal possessed a shortened skull with a broadened rear section and eyes directed forward.
The snout of the creature was notably short, accounting for less than two-thirds of the total skull length.
This unique anatomy included a narrow snout, a wide posterior skull, and forward-facing eyes that were rare for the time.
Its powerful bite force was strong enough to crush bone, not merely to slice through flesh.
The shape of its teeth allowed it to tear off huge chunks of meat and bone to swallow them whole.
The species was formally described by Loewen and colleagues in the year 2013.
The single known specimen was found in 2009 within the Wahweap Formation of the Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument in Utah.
Paleontologist Mark A. Loewen and his team designated specimen UMNH VP 20200 as the holotype for Lythronax argestes in 2013.
This holotype was recovered from locality UMNH VP 1501, a specific site within the Wahweap Formation in Kane County, southern Utah.
Based on its stratigraphic position, Lythronax argestes is recognized as the oldest known tyrannosaurid.
Lythronax was likely the largest predator within its specific ecosystem.
The animal had forward-facing eyes that provided depth perception, a trait likely useful for hunting.
In 2006, Kent Stevens suggested that such forward-directed orbits aided Tyrannosaurus in either pursuit or ambush predation.
This skull anatomy would have given Lythronax binocular vision, allowing it to perceive depth, a condition considered predatory.
As a tyrannosaurid, it likely possessed a large body size, powerful jaw muscles, robust teeth, reinforced skull sutures, and small forelimbs.
It is suggested that Lythronax's teeth were used not only to cut meat but also to inflict damage and break bones.
Vertebrates living in the same habitat included freshwater fish, bowfins, rays, sharks, turtles like Compsemys, crocodilians, and lungfish.
Numerous mammals also lived in the region, including multituberculates, cladotherians, marsupials, and placental insectivores.
Lythronax belongs to the family Tyrannosauridae, which consists of large-bodied coelurosaurs.
The species is further classified within the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae.
The full scientific name of the animal is Lythronax argestes.
The generic name Lythronax is derived from the Greek words for gore and king.
The specific name argestes refers to the southwest wind named by Homer, alluding to the specimen's location in North America.
Lythronax lived during the Campanian stage in the Western Interior Basin.
The rocks containing Lythronax fossils are estimated to be 81.49 million years old, with an uncertainty range of 81.86 to 81.45 million years.
Lythronax lived approximately 80 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
The environment where Lythronax lived included lakes, floodplains, and rivers that flowed east.
The discovery of Lythronax suggests that forward-directed orbits appeared in tyrannosauroids by at least 80 million years ago.
Gregory S. Paul suggested that Lythronax argestes might belong to the genus Tyrannosaurus, arguing that derived tyrannosaurids are oversplit.
It is debated whether differences in phylogenetic results stem from an over-weighting of certain features by Loewen and colleagues.
It is debated whether Tyrannosaurus originated from Asian tyrannosaurids or from southern Laramidian tyrannosaurids.
